\caption{Robustness of the screen to the quantum kernel (upper block) and to the classical kernel used to compute alignment (lower block). In the upper block, alignment is the classical RBF alignment of the paper and the quantum kernel changes; the six kernels are evaluated on identical seed-42 features at $N=1000$ for all 30 configurations, and the first row reproduces the paper's kernel. In the lower block, the quantum kernel is the paper's and the classical kernel behind $A_C$ changes. For each setting the table gives the correlation $r$ between alignment and the utility gap, the number $n$ of configurations flagged at $A_C<0.05$, and the largest gap among them, which is the most a practitioner following the rule would give up. On the main grid, $r$ is significant ($p<0.01$) for the four eight-qubit kernels and for every classical kernel, and on the hold-out it is significant at the $0.05$ level for none. With 6 and 4 qubits, only the first $k$ of the eight features enter the quantum kernel while $A_C$ is computed on all eight. Row tint groups the settings, the four eight-qubit circuits, the two reduced-qubit circuits, and the classical kernels.}
